items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the area of land drained by a river and its tributaries, bounded by a watershed”.
items.answer: Drainage basin
items.markingKey: Drainage basin: the area of land drained by a river and its tributaries, bounded by a watershed. [1]

items.stem: Explain why the drainage basin is regarded as an open system while the global hydrological cycle is a closed system.
items.answer: The basin receives precipitation from outside and loses water by evapotranspiration and channel discharge across its boundary; the global cycle has a fixed amount of water that only moves between stores (oceans, atmosphere, ice, land).
items.markingKey: 1 mark inputs/outputs of basin; 1 mark fixed global water; 1 mark energy still crosses the global boundary [3]

items.stem: Describe the pathways by which precipitation falling on a forested drainage basin may reach the river channel.
items.answer: Intercepted then throughfall or stemflow to the ground; infiltration into the soil and throughflow downslope; percolation to groundwater and slow baseflow; overland flow when the soil is saturated or rainfall intense; direct channel precipitation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per pathway, max 2 if no sequence [4]

items.stem: A student draws a flow diagram of the drainage basin system for a small upland catchment in the Pennines, UK, with peat moorland on impermeable gritstone. Distinguish between infiltration and percolation.
items.answer: Infiltration is water entering the soil surface; percolation is water moving down from the soil into the rock below.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A student draws a flow diagram of the drainage basin system for a small upland catchment in the Pennines, UK, with peat moorland on impermeable gritstone. (a) Name two stores shown in the system. (b) Suggest how one human activity could increase the output of water from this basin.
items.answer: (a) Any two of: interception, surface (depression) storage, soil moisture, groundwater, channel storage. (b) Drainage ditches (gripping) on the moor or clearing vegetation speed flows and increase discharge; reservoirs may increase evaporation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark activity; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.1 is a systems diagram of a drainage basin. It shows inputs (precipitation), stores (interception, surface, soil, groundwater, channel) and transfers (throughfall, stemflow, infiltration, percolation, throughflow, overland flow, baseflow) and outputs (evapotranspiration, discharge). (a) Name two stores shown in the system. (b) Distinguish between infiltration and percolation.
items.answer: (a) Any two of: interception, surface (depression) storage, soil moisture, groundwater, channel storage. (b) Infiltration is water entering the soil surface; percolation is water moving down from the soil into the rock below.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A student draws a flow diagram of the drainage basin system for a small upland catchment in the Pennines, UK, with peat moorland on impermeable gritstone. (a) Explain why channel discharge continues during rainless periods in some basins. (b) Suggest how one human activity could increase the output of water from this basin.
items.answer: (a) Baseflow from groundwater and slow throughflow from the soil continue to supply the channel. (b) Drainage ditches (gripping) on the moor or clearing vegetation speed flows and increase discharge; reservoirs may increase evaporation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark baseflow; 1 mark source [2] (b) 1 mark activity; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.1 is a systems diagram of a drainage basin. It shows inputs (precipitation), stores (interception, surface, soil, groundwater, channel) and transfers (throughfall, stemflow, infiltration, percolation, throughflow, overland flow, baseflow) and outputs (evapotranspiration, discharge). (a) Explain how saturated peat on impermeable rock would affect the transfers shown. (b) Explain why channel discharge continues during rainless periods in some basins.
items.answer: (a) Infiltration and percolation are low; most water moves as saturated overland flow or throughflow in the peat; little groundwater and baseflow, so rapid flood peaks. (b) Baseflow from groundwater and slow throughflow from the soil continue to supply the channel.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per developed point [3] (b) 1 mark baseflow; 1 mark source [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “drainage basin”?
options: The combined loss of water to the atmosphere by evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants.
The area of land drained by a river and its tributaries, bounded by a watershed.
A system that receives inputs from, and loses outputs to, outside its boundary, as the drainage basin does.
The boundary of a drainage basin, usually a ridge of high land separating one basin from the next.
items.answer: The area of land drained by a river and its tributaries, bounded by a watershed.
items.markingKey: Drainage basin: the area of land drained by a river and its tributaries, bounded by a watershed. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “All precipitation that falls in a drainage basin eventually leaves as river discharge.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Much is lost by evapotranspiration and some is held in long-term stores such as deep groundwater or ice.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how the size of the groundwater store affects river flow during a dry season.
items.answer: Groundwater drains slowly into the channel as baseflow; a large aquifer (e.g. permeable chalk or sandstone) maintains flow during dry months, whereas impermeable basins have little store and rivers may dry up.
items.markingKey: 1 mark baseflow; 1 mark slow release; 1 mark rock type example [3]

items.stem: Table 1.1 gives annual water balance data for part of the River Ouse (UK) catchment (area 250 km²): precipitation 1 770 mm, evapotranspiration 650 mm, and an estimated change in storage of +60 mm. Using P = Q + E ± ΔS, what is the runoff (Q) in mm?
Briefly explain how human activities have changed the drainage basin system, for the River Severn basin, UK or another example of a drainage basin.
items.answer: the River Severn basin, UK: Reservoirs (Clywedog, Vyrnwy) regulate flow; urban growth at Shrewsbury and Worcester increases runoff; conifer plantations on Plynlimon increased interception; flood barriers at Bewdley and Shrewsbury.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Land-use change, dams, abstraction, urbanisation; effects on named stores and flows. [5]

items.stem: Briefly explain how human activities have changed the drainage basin system, for the Amazon basin, South America or another example of a drainage basin.
items.answer: the Amazon basin, South America: Deforestation for cattle ranching and soya (e.g. in Mato Grosso and Rondônia) reduces interception and evapotranspiration; research suggests reduced recycling of moisture lowers rainfall downwind and lengthens the dry season; dams such as Belo Monte on the Xingu alter channel flow.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Land-use change, dams, abstraction, urbanisation; effects on named stores and flows. [5]

items.stem: Referring to the River Severn basin, UK or another example of a drainage basin, assess the extent to which human activities have changed the stores and flows of the drainage basin.
items.answer: Model answer (the River Severn basin, UK): About 11 400 km²; rises on Plynlimon in Wales (over 2000 mm rain a year on impermeable rocks with peat) and flows about 350 km to the Bristol Channel; mean discharge about 107 m³/s at Bewdley; lower basin has permeable sandstones that store groundwater. Reservoirs (Clywedog, Vyrnwy) regulate flow; urban growth at Shrewsbury and Worcester increases runoff; conifer plantations on Plynlimon increased interception; flood barriers at Bewdley and Shrewsbury.

items.stem: “Human activity has a greater effect than physical factors on the transfers of water within a drainage basin.” How far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Urbanisation replaces permeable soil with concrete, cutting infiltration; deforestation removes interception; field drains and channelisation speed throughflow and channel flow. Against: Rock permeability, soil type, slope and vegetation set the basic pattern of transfers; climate (rainfall intensity, frozen ground) controls overland flow in most basins. Conclusion: Physical factors set the baseline in all basins, but in heavily modified (urban or deforested) basins human activity dominates transfers.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the capture and temporary storage of precipitation by vegetation before it reaches the ground”.
items.answer: Interception
items.markingKey: Interception: the capture and temporary storage of precipitation by vegetation before it reaches the ground. [1]

items.stem: Explain why infiltration rates decrease during a long period of rainfall.
items.answer: Soil pores fill and the soil approaches saturation; raindrop impact seals the surface (crusting); swelling clays close cracks; so infiltration falls towards a steady rate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed point [3]

items.stem: Explain the factors that influence the amount of interception.
items.answer: Vegetation type and density (conifers > deciduous > grass); season (leaf cover); rainfall intensity and duration (light rain mostly intercepted, storage capacity filled in long storms); wind speed and evaporation between showers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor with explanation [4]

items.stem: Arjun measured rainfall in a storm in a maize field in Kenya. A rain gauge in a nearby clearing collected 23 mm; gauges below the canopy recorded a mean throughfall of 19.7 mm and stemflow collars recorded the equivalent of 1.4 mm. Suggest how the percentage would differ in a longer, more intense storm. Explain your answer.
items.answer: Lower percentage: the canopy storage capacity is soon filled, so once leaves are saturated most extra rain becomes throughfall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark lower; 1 mark storage capacity [2]

items.stem: Omar measured rainfall in a storm in a maize field in Kenya. A rain gauge in a nearby clearing collected 30 mm; gauges below the canopy recorded a mean throughfall of 24.3 mm and stemflow collars recorded the equivalent of 2.1 mm. (a) Calculate the interception loss in mm. (b) Calculate the interception loss as a percentage of gross rainfall.
items.markingKey: (a) gross rainfall − (throughfall + stemflow) = 30 − (24.3 + 2.1) = 3.6 [1] (b) 3.6 ÷ 30 × 100 = 12% [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that vegetation is the most important factor controlling how much precipitation infiltrates into the soil?
items.answer: For: Vegetation intercepts rain and slows its arrival; roots and soil fauna create macropores; litter protects soil from crusting; forest soils have very high infiltration capacities. Against: Soil texture and structure (sand v clay), antecedent moisture, rainfall intensity, slope angle, frozen ground and urban surfaces can override vegetation. Conclusion: Vegetation is very important in natural basins, but rainfall intensity and soil conditions (saturation, frost, compaction) often determine infiltration during storms.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “precipitation that drips from leaves or falls through gaps in the canopy to the ground”.
items.answer: Throughfall
items.markingKey: Throughfall: precipitation that drips from leaves or falls through gaps in the canopy to the ground. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Interception is the same in a deciduous forest throughout the year.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. In winter, leafless deciduous trees intercept far less than in summer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why stemflow is a larger proportion of rainfall under some trees than others.
items.answer: Branches angled upwards and smooth bark channel water to the trunk (e.g. beech); rough bark and drooping branches lead to more throughfall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark branch architecture; 1 mark bark [2]

items.stem: A ring infiltrometer was used on a school playing field. The infiltration rates recorded (mm/h) after 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 30 minutes were: 72, 51, 40, 33, 29, 27. Calculate the percentage decrease in infiltration rate between 0 and 30 minutes.

Leila measured rainfall in a storm in a coniferous (Sitka spruce) plantation in Scotland. A rain gauge in a nearby clearing collected 51 mm; gauges below the canopy recorded a mean throughfall of 34.5 mm and stemflow collars recorded the equivalent of 1.6 mm. (a) Calculate the interception loss as a percentage of gross rainfall. (b) Explain how the interception loss affects the shape of the river’s storm hydrograph.
items.answer: (a) 29.2% (b) Less water reaches the ground and it arrives more slowly, so lag time increases and peak discharge is lower.

items.stem: Samuel measured rainfall in a storm in a deciduous oak woodland in summer. A rain gauge in a nearby clearing collected 79 mm; gauges below the canopy recorded a mean throughfall of 55.8 mm and stemflow collars recorded the equivalent of 4.2 mm. (a) Suggest how the percentage would differ in a longer, more intense storm. Explain your answer. (b) Suggest two sources of error in this method.
items.answer: (a) Lower percentage: the canopy storage capacity is soon filled, so once leaves are saturated most extra rain becomes throughfall. (b) Gauges sample only a few points under a patchy canopy; splash in or out of gauges; evaporation from gauges; stemflow collars leak; the clearing gauge may be affected by nearby trees.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark lower; 1 mark storage capacity [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “water that flows across the ground surface when rainfall exceeds infiltration capacity or the soil is saturated”.
items.answer: Overland flow
items.markingKey: Overland flow: water that flows across the ground surface when rainfall exceeds infiltration capacity or the soil is saturated. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between infiltration-excess and saturation-excess overland flow.
items.answer: Infiltration-excess (Hortonian) occurs when rainfall intensity exceeds infiltration capacity, common on bare or compacted ground in intense storms; saturation-excess occurs when the soil is full, even in light rain, commonly on footslopes and valley floors.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each definition; 1 mark location/condition [3]

items.stem: Explain the annual pattern of soil moisture in a temperate climate such as the UK.
items.answer: Winter surplus when precipitation exceeds evapotranspiration; spring/summer utilisation as evapotranspiration rises and soil water is used; late summer deficit; autumn recharge as evapotranspiration falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage in order [4]

items.stem: Name a case study of groundwater depletion you have studied. For your example, explain why the groundwater store has been depleted.
items.answer: the Punjab and Haryana aquifers, north-west India: Free or subsidised electricity for pumps since the Green Revolution; over a million tube wells; rice and wheat double cropping needs heavy irrigation; groundwater use exceeds recharge.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Abstraction > recharge; irrigation, pricing, crops, climate. [5]

items.stem: Table 1.3 shows mean monthly precipitation (P) and potential evapotranspiration (PE), in mm, for a station in central France. Jan: P 74, PE 0. Feb: P 80, PE 15. Mar: P 45, PE 27. Apr: P 48, PE 51. May: P 56, PE 73. Jun: P 58, PE 95. Jul: P 51, PE 109. Aug: P 58, PE 90. Sep: P 50, PE 61. Oct: P 77, PE 39. Nov: P 91, PE 19. Dec: P 80, PE 10. (a) Identify the months in which there is a water deficit (PE > P). (b) Explain why river discharge is likely to be highest in winter at this station even though monthly precipitation is similar all year.
items.answer: (a) Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep (b) PE is low in winter so more of the precipitation becomes runoff; soils are at field capacity, so infiltration is limited and recharge feeds baseflow.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for all correct, 1 mark if one error [2] (b) 1 mark low PE; 1 mark saturated soils/recharge [2]

items.stem: With reference to a case study of groundwater depletion, evaluate the effectiveness of attempts to manage groundwater.
items.answer: Model answer (the Ogallala aquifer, Great Plains, USA): Centre-pivot irrigation for maize and cattle feed across eight states draws water stored over thousands of years; recharge in the semi-arid southern plains is very slow. Water levels down by more than 30 m in parts of Kansas and Texas; some farms have returned to dryland farming; local conservation districts limit pumping.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the lateral movement of water downslope through the soil”.
items.answer: Throughflow
items.markingKey: Throughflow: the lateral movement of water downslope through the soil. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Groundwater stores can take many years to recover once they are depleted.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Recharge by percolation is slow; for example, aquifers under the North China Plain and Punjab have fallen for decades.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why groundwater abstraction can lead to rivers drying up.
items.answer: Lowering the water table below the river bed reduces or reverses baseflow, so in dry periods there is no supply to the channel.
items.markingKey: 1 mark water table; 1 mark baseflow [2]

items.stem: Table 1.3 shows mean monthly precipitation (P) and potential evapotranspiration (PE), in mm, for a station in southern England. Jan: P 77, PE 7. Feb: P 83, PE 11. Mar: P 50, PE 27. Apr: P 72, PE 50. May: P 80, PE 77. Jun: P 62, PE 94. Jul: P 55, PE 106. Aug: P 52, PE 92. Sep: P 56, PE 59. Oct: P 53, PE 38. Nov: P 73, PE 15. Dec: P 48, PE 1. Explain why river discharge is likely to be highest in winter at this station even though monthly precipitation is similar all year.
items.answer: PE is low in winter so more of the precipitation becomes runoff; soils are at field capacity, so infiltration is limited and recharge feeds baseflow.
items.markingKey: 1 mark low PE; 1 mark saturated soils/recharge [2]

items.stem: Table 1.3 shows mean monthly precipitation (P) and potential evapotranspiration (PE), in mm, for a station in central France. Jan: P 65, PE 10. Feb: P 94, PE 8. Mar: P 49, PE 29. items.answer: (a) P = 792 mm; PE = 589 mm (b) Apr, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep (c) 332 mm
items.markingKey: (a) sum of monthly values [2] (b) 1 mark for all correct, 1 mark if one error [2] (c) sum of (P − PE) for surplus months [2]

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that groundwater is the most important store in determining river flow. In your answer you may refer to baseflow and snow and ice.
items.answer: For: Baseflow from aquifers maintains discharge in dry periods; chalk rivers such as the Test flow steadily; groundwater stores regulate regimes. Against: In impermeable or urban basins overland flow and throughflow dominate storm response; snow and glacier stores dominate regimes in mountain basins; soil moisture controls storm runoff. Conclusion: Groundwater controls low flows and stable regimes in permeable basins, but other stores matter more for storm flows and in impermeable or glacial basins.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the boundary of a drainage basin, usually a ridge of high land separating one basin from the next”.
items.answer: Watershed
items.markingKey: Watershed: the boundary of a drainage basin, usually a ridge of high land separating one basin from the next. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Throughflow is usually slower than overland flow.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Water moving through soil pores meets more resistance than water flowing over the surface.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how deforestation alters stores and flows in a drainage basin.
items.answer: Less interception storage and transpiration; more rain reaches the ground quickly; soil compaction lowers infiltration so more overland flow; less soil moisture and groundwater recharge; faster channel flow and higher flood peaks.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed change [4]

items.stem: Table 1.1 gives annual water balance data for part of the Mekong tributary (Laos) catchment (area 250 km²): precipitation 1 550 mm, evapotranspiration 740 mm, and an estimated change in storage of −20 mm. (a) Calculate the runoff as a percentage of precipitation (the runoff coefficient). (b) State what a negative change in storage suggests about the year.
items.answer: (a) 53.5% (b) Stores (soil moisture, groundwater) were drawn down: a drier than average year or heavy abstraction.

items.stem: Using one named example of a drainage basin, explain how human activities have changed the drainage basin system.
items.answer: the River Severn basin, UK: Reservoirs (Clywedog, Vyrnwy) regulate flow; urban growth at Shrewsbury and Worcester increases runoff; conifer plantations on Plynlimon increased interception; flood barriers at Bewdley and Shrewsbury.

items.answer: 980 mm

items.stem: With reference to a case study of a drainage basin, evaluate whether physical or human factors have the greater influence on the drainage basin system.
items.answer: Model answer (the Amazon basin, South America): About 7 million km² with annual rainfall of 2000-3000 mm; around half of precipitation is recycled by evapotranspiration from the rainforest; mean discharge at the mouth about 200 000 m³/s, about 15-20% of all river water entering the oceans. items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “water that flows down branches and trunks to the ground”.
items.answer: Stemflow
items.markingKey: Stemflow: water that flows down branches and trunks to the ground. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Saturated soils can produce overland flow even when rainfall intensity is low.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Saturation-excess overland flow occurs when there is no pore space left, whatever the rainfall rate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how land use affects infiltration.
items.answer: Forest litter and roots keep pores open (high infiltration); grazing and machinery compact soil; ploughing may increase it temporarily; urban surfaces are impermeable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per land use explained [3]

items.stem: Leila measured rainfall in a storm in a tropical rainforest in Sabah, Malaysia. A rain gauge in a nearby clearing collected 35 mm; gauges below the canopy recorded a mean throughfall of 26.3 mm and stemflow collars recorded the equivalent of 0.4 mm. Explain how the interception loss affects the shape of the river’s storm hydrograph.
items.answer: Less water reaches the ground and it arrives more slowly, so lag time increases and peak discharge is lower.
items.markingKey: 1 mark lag; 1 mark peak [2]

items.stem: A ring infiltrometer was used on arable land after harvest. The infiltration rates recorded (mm/h) after 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 30 minutes were: 88, 60, 49, 40, 35, 31. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in infiltration rate between 0 and 30 minutes. (b) Suggest why the steady infiltration rate here may differ from that of an ungrazed woodland.
items.answer: (a) 64.8% (b) Compaction by trampling, livestock or machinery reduces pore spaces; less organic matter and fewer roots and burrows; woodland litter protects the surface.
items.markingKey: (a) (88 − 31) ÷ 88 × 100 = 64.8% [2] (b) 1 mark compaction; 1 mark roots/organic matter [2]

items.stem: “Vegetation is the most important factor controlling how much precipitation infiltrates into the soil.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to antecedent conditions, rainfall intensity and soil type.
items.answer: For: Vegetation intercepts rain and slows its arrival; roots and soil fauna create macropores; litter protects soil from crusting; forest soils have very high infiltration capacities. Against: Soil texture and structure (sand v clay), antecedent moisture, rainfall intensity, slope angle, frozen ground and urban surfaces can override vegetation. Conclusion: Vegetation is very important in natural basins, but rainfall intensity and soil conditions (saturation, frost, compaction) often determine infiltration during storms.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “overland flow”?
options: The part of river discharge supplied by groundwater, which maintains flow between storms.
The lateral movement of water downslope through the soil.
Water that flows across the ground surface when rainfall exceeds infiltration capacity or the soil is saturated.
The slow movement of water through permeable rock below the water table.
items.answer: Water that flows across the ground surface when rainfall exceeds infiltration capacity or the soil is saturated.
items.markingKey: Overland flow: water that flows across the ground surface when rainfall exceeds infiltration capacity or the soil is saturated. [1]

items.stem: Explain how soil type affects throughflow.
items.answer: Sandy soils with large pores transmit water quickly; clays have small pores and slow throughflow; pipes and macropores (roots, cracks) allow rapid pipeflow.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each point [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Groundwater stores can take many years to recover once they are depleted.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Overland flow is the main route by which water reaches rivers in most humid temperate basins.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Recharge by percolation is slow; for example, aquifers under the North China Plain and Punjab have fallen for decades. (b) Not correct. In vegetated humid basins most water reaches rivers by throughflow and groundwater flow; overland flow is local.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Using one named example of groundwater depletion, explain why the groundwater store has been depleted.
items.answer: the Ogallala aquifer, Great Plains, USA: Centre-pivot irrigation for maize and cattle feed across eight states draws water stored over thousands of years; recharge in the semi-arid southern plains is very slow.

items.stem: Name a case study of groundwater depletion you have studied. For your example, describe the impacts of falling groundwater levels.
items.answer: the Punjab and Haryana aquifers, north-west India: Water tables falling by about 0.5-1 m a year in many districts; farmers must deepen wells at high cost; reduced baseflow; arsenic and salinity problems; schemes to delay rice transplanting to reduce pumping.

items.stem: Referring to the Ogallala aquifer, Great Plains, USA or another example of groundwater depletion, evaluate the effectiveness of attempts to manage groundwater.
items.answer: Model answer (the Ogallala aquifer, Great Plains, USA): Centre-pivot irrigation for maize and cattle feed across eight states draws water stored over thousands of years; recharge in the semi-arid southern plains is very slow. Water levels down by more than 30 m in parts of Kansas and Texas; some farms have returned to dryland farming; local conservation districts limit pumping.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a system that receives inputs from, and loses outputs to, outside its boundary, as the drainage basin does”.
items.answer: Open system

items.stem: A revision website states: “A watershed is a store of water at the head of a valley.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. A watershed is the boundary (divide) of a drainage basin, not a store.

items.stem: Classify each of the following components of the drainage basin system as an input, output, store or flow (transfer): overland flow; soil moisture; precipitation; channel storage; percolation; stemflow.
items.answer: overland flow: flow; soil moisture: store; precipitation: input; channel storage: store; percolation: flow; stemflow: flow

items.stem: Table 1.1 gives annual water balance data for part of the River Ouse (UK) catchment (area 1 500 km²): precipitation 1 940 mm, evapotranspiration 620 mm, and an estimated change in storage of +60 mm. Suggest two reasons why evapotranspiration varies between drainage basins.
items.answer: Temperature and insolation; vegetation type and density (transpiration); wind speed and humidity; water availability; surface type.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.1 is a systems diagram of a drainage basin. It shows inputs (precipitation), stores (interception, surface, soil, groundwater, channel) and transfers (throughfall, stemflow, infiltration, percolation, throughflow, overland flow, baseflow) and outputs (evapotranspiration, discharge). (a) Name two stores shown in the system. (b) Explain how saturated peat on impermeable rock would affect the transfers shown.
items.answer: (a) Any two of: interception, surface (depression) storage, soil moisture, groundwater, channel storage. (b) Infiltration and percolation are low; most water moves as saturated overland flow or throughflow in the peat; little groundwater and baseflow, so rapid flood peaks.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark per developed point [3]

items.stem: Using a named example of a drainage basin you have studied, evaluate whether physical or human factors have the greater influence on the drainage basin system.
items.answer: Model answer (the Amazon basin, South America): About 7 million km² with annual rainfall of 2000-3000 mm; around half of precipitation is recycled by evapotranspiration from the rainforest; mean discharge at the mouth about 200 000 m³/s, about 15-20% of all river water entering the oceans. Deforestation for cattle ranching and soya (e.g. in Mato Grosso and Rondônia) reduces interception and evapotranspiration; research suggests reduced recycling of moisture lowers rainfall downwind and lengthens the dry season; dams such as Belo Monte on the Xingu alter channel flow.

items.stem: Assess the view that human activity has a greater effect than physical factors on the transfers of water within a drainage basin.
items.answer: For: Urbanisation replaces permeable soil with concrete, cutting infiltration; deforestation removes interception; field drains and channelisation speed throughflow and channel flow. Against: Rock permeability, soil type, slope and vegetation set the basic pattern of transfers; climate (rainfall intensity, frozen ground) controls overland flow in most basins. Conclusion: Physical factors set the baseline in all basins, but in heavily modified (urban or deforested) basins human activity dominates transfers.

items.answer: Infiltration

items.stem: A revision website states: “Stemflow increases the amount of water reaching the ground directly around tree trunks.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. It concentrates water at the base of the trunk, where infiltration can be high along roots.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “Stemflow increases the amount of water reaching the ground directly around tree trunks.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why infiltration rates decrease during a long period of rainfall.
items.answer: (a) Correct. It concentrates water at the base of the trunk, where infiltration can be high along roots. (b) Soil pores fill and the soil approaches saturation; raindrop impact seals the surface (crusting); swelling clays close cracks; so infiltration falls towards a steady rate.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per developed point [3]

items.stem: A ring infiltrometer was used on an ungrazed woodland. The infiltration rates recorded (mm/h) after 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 30 minutes were: 186, 123, 91, 77, 72, 64. Calculate the percentage decrease in infiltration rate between 0 and 30 minutes.

Leila measured rainfall in a storm in a eucalyptus plantation in Brazil. A rain gauge in a nearby clearing collected 73 mm; gauges below the canopy recorded a mean throughfall of 62.3 mm and stemflow collars recorded the equivalent of 1.5 mm. (a) Calculate the interception loss as a percentage of gross rainfall. (b) Suggest two sources of error in this method.
items.answer: (a) 12.6% (b) Gauges sample only a few points under a patchy canopy; splash in or out of gauges; evaporation from gauges; stemflow collars leak; the clearing gauge may be affected by nearby trees.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why groundwater abstraction can lead to rivers drying up. (b) A revision website states: “A soil moisture deficit means the soil is completely dry.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Lowering the water table below the river bed reduces or reverses baseflow, so in dry periods there is no supply to the channel. (b) Not correct. It means the soil holds less than field capacity; it may still contain water.

items.stem: “Groundwater is the most important store in determining river flow.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to snow and ice, soil moisture and baseflow.
items.answer: For: Baseflow from aquifers maintains discharge in dry periods; chalk rivers such as the Test flow steadily; groundwater stores regulate regimes. Against: In impermeable or urban basins overland flow and throughflow dominate storm response; snow and glacier stores dominate regimes in mountain basins; soil moisture controls storm runoff. Conclusion: Groundwater controls low flows and stable regimes in permeable basins, but other stores matter more for storm flows and in impermeable or glacial basins.
